task.goal: Help first-time library volunteers handle a disagreement about a shared room booking without taking sides prematurely.
hard_constraints: A 45-minute training with role cards and one facilitator.
Do not ask trainees to recount personal conflicts; no legal or disciplinary advice.
Practice must include verifying the booking record, listening to both parties, and knowing when to escalate; assess an unseen scenario individually.
task.available_resources: Fictional booking records and policy excerpt.
task.expected_result: A role-play sequence and actionable escalation check.

DIRECT_FULL.title: A three-gate conversation protocol
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Mechanism: give novices three gates—hear both accounts, verify the record, then resolve or escalate. Requiring observable evidence before a decision could reduce premature siding, although trainees may follow the sequence mechanically.

Use 45 minutes: 0–5 introduce neutrality and the fictional policy; 5–10 the facilitator demonstrates the gates; 10–28 run three six-minute role-play rounds in triads, rotating volunteer and two room users; 28–35 discuss missed gates and repeat difficult moments; 35–43 complete an unseen individual scenario; 43–45 review the escalation check. Nobody recounts personal conflicts.

Role cards give each room user a plausible claim, one relevant detail, and an immediate need. The volunteer receives the booking record and policy excerpt. Each round includes listening to both parties, summarizing each account without endorsing it, checking room/date/time/status in the record, explaining what is established, and proposing only policy-supported next steps.

Actionable escalation check: Is there an immediate safety concern? Follow the excerpt’s safety route. Is the record missing, contradictory, or insufficient? Pause allocation and contact the designated staff member. Does the requested exception exceed volunteer authority, or does disagreement persist after clarification? Escalate with both accounts, verified facts, unresolved questions, and the next update time. Avoid blame, sanctions, and legal conclusions.

Needs: one facilitator, printed role cards, fictional records, and an excerpt specifying volunteer authority and a staff contact route. Assume enough trainees for triads; a pair can alternate the second claimant role. The protocol cannot settle ambiguities the policy leaves unresolved.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Use two matched unseen written scenarios, counterbalanced across trainees: one answered before instruction using ordinary judgment, one afterward using the gates. Score record verification, fair hearing, and justified escalation separately. A minimal falsifying result is that protocol users still allocate the room before hearing both claims, or escalate clear routine cases without justification. This small comparison checks usability and immediate performance, not lasting transfer.

DIRECT_FULL.title: An evidence-gap role-play
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Mechanism: distribute incomplete but compatible information across the two claimants and the booking record. The volunteer can reach a defensible next step only by asking both parties questions and cross-checking the record. This makes impartial listening useful for solving the task, rather than merely a courtesy.

Allocate 45 minutes: 0–5 explain the fictional policy and boundaries; 5–9 demonstrate separating a claim from a verified fact; 9–27 run three six-minute triad rounds with rotating roles; 27–34 reveal the evidence and discuss unsupported assumptions; 34–42 assess an unseen case individually; 42–45 rehearse escalation handoffs. Use fictional situations exclusively.

Each claimant card states what to disclose initially and what to disclose when asked. For example, one person has a confirmation for a different room; the other has the correct room but an outdated time. The booking record establishes current status. Later rounds include a genuinely unresolved discrepancy so that finding more information does not always produce a volunteer-level resolution. Volunteers must hear both accounts and inspect the record in every round.

The escalation check asks: Can I establish the booking from the available record? Does the policy authorize my proposed next step? Can the interaction continue safely and constructively? If any answer is no, use the excerpt’s designated staff route. State what each person reports, what the record confirms, what remains uncertain, and what assistance is needed. Do not assign fault or invent consequences.

Needs: one facilitator, coordinated role cards and records, and a policy excerpt defining authority and escalation contacts. Card preparation requires care: avoid trick wording and ensure information becomes available through reasonable questions. Limits include reading demands and trainees learning to hunt for hidden clues rather than listen naturally.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Compare one ordinary full-information practice case with one evidence-gap case, counterbalancing order. Then give everyone the same unseen individual case with both accounts and a record available. Check whether trainees identify the decisive discrepancy, acknowledge both accounts, and choose a supported action. The mechanism is weakened if evidence-gap practice produces more guessing or clue-hunting without better verification than ordinary practice.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Pause, compare, and replay decision points
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Mechanism: rehearse the moment when a volunteer is tempted to decide too early. Short pauses let trainees compare a premature response with an evidence-seeking response, then immediately replay the conversation. The intended change is recognition of decision hazards under pressure; improvement is uncertain until tested without pauses.

Use 45 minutes: 0–5 introduce policy and respectful boundaries; 5–10 the facilitator models a rushed decision and invites a replacement line; 10–28 triads complete three six-minute rounds, rotating volunteer and two claimants; 28–34 review decision points; 34–42 complete an unseen individual assessment; 42–45 review the escalation check. All examples are fictional, with no requests for personal experiences.

Role cards introduce distinct pressures: an apparently confident claimant, an urgent request, or two conflicting confirmations. Every round requires listening to both parties and inspecting the booking record. A printed pause marker appears after the opening claims and after record inspection. At each marker the volunteer states what is known, what remains unverified, and the next question or action. The triad briefly compares two responses, selects the policy-supported response, and replays from the marker. The facilitator circulates and corrects substantive misunderstandings.

Actionable escalation check: stop and use the policy’s safety route for immediate safety concerns; seek designated staff when records conflict, authority is insufficient, or disagreement persists after a clear explanation. Give a neutral handoff containing both accounts, verified booking details, the unresolved issue, and the requested staff decision. Avoid disciplinary or legal advice.

Needs: one facilitator, role cards with pause markers, fictional records, and an excerpt defining escalation routes. Assume trainees can use the markers without constant facilitator supervision. Pauses may make practice easier than real service, so the final assessment removes them.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Have trainees first answer a brief unseen case without prompts, then assess a matched unseen case individually after rehearsal. Require their opening response, record checks, summaries of both accounts, and escalation decision. Compare against the simple pretraining response. A falsifying signal is successful prompted replay followed by premature siding or unsupported decisions when markers disappear; that would suggest dependence on rehearsal cues rather than transferable judgment.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Reverse the claimants, preserve the facts
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Mechanism: replay the same dispute after swapping the claimants’ presentation styles while preserving every booking fact. A confident, familiar-sounding claimant becomes hesitant; the other becomes assertive. Comparing the volunteer’s responses makes reliance on confidence or apparent familiarity visible. The intended change is a more stable judgment based on verified facts and both accounts, rather than personal impressions. This differs from simply rotating practice roles: the controlled reversal is the teaching device.

Use 45 minutes: 0–6 introduce the fictional policy and boundaries; 6–10 explain role cards and neutral opening language; 10–28 run three six-minute triad cycles, rotating the volunteer. Each cycle includes a short encounter, a replay with claimant styles reversed, and comparison. Use 28–33 to discuss which responses changed and why; 33–42 for an unseen individual assessment; 42–45 for the escalation check. Use fictional disputes only; offer no legal or disciplinary advice.

Both versions require the volunteer to hear each party, summarize their accounts, and verify room, date, time, and booking status against the record. Cards specify identical substantive information across versions, disclosed without requiring clever questions. Respectful listening should remain consistent even when delivery changes.

Escalation check: follow the excerpt’s safety route for immediate danger; contact designated staff if records remain contradictory, a requested action exceeds volunteer authority, or disagreement persists after explanation. Hand over both accounts, verified details, the unresolved question, and the assistance needed.

Needs: one facilitator, paired role cards, fictional records, and an excerpt defining authority and staff contacts. Triads must manage timing independently. Style changes should avoid identity stereotypes. Repetition may itself improve performance, and trainees may recognize the lesson without transferring it to service.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: In a small pilot, give some triads a style-reversal replay and others an identical replay, with equal practice time. Everyone then answers the same unseen scenario individually, stating their opening response, questions for both parties, record checks, and escalation decision. Compare premature allocation and unsupported reliance on confidence. The mechanism is weakened if reversal practice produces no improvement over ordinary repetition, or merely makes trainees favor the quieter claimant. This checks immediate transfer, not durable behavior.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Learn the boundary through contrasting cases
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Mechanism: teach volunteers to distinguish cases they can handle from cases requiring staff by comparing closely matched disputes whose decisive difference is authority or evidence quality. Contrast can expose the actual escalation boundary: a clear record supports one action, while an unresolved discrepancy or unauthorized exception requires staff. This aims to prevent both premature decisions and automatic escalation of every disagreement.

Use 45 minutes: 0–5 introduce the fictional policy and boundaries; 5–11 compare two short case files differing in one decisive fact; 11–29 run three six-minute triad role-plays, rotating volunteer and two claimants; 29–34 compare decisions against the excerpt; 34–42 assess an unseen scenario individually; 42–45 rehearse a staff handoff. All situations are fictional; do not solicit personal conflicts or provide legal or disciplinary advice.

Prepare three practice packets: a routine case with a clear current booking, a matched case with conflicting current records, and a clear booking accompanied by an exception request outside volunteer authority. Role cards give both claimants reasonable concerns. In every encounter, volunteers listen to both parties and verify room, date, time, and status before choosing a next step. Trainees explain which specific fact or policy provision permits action or requires escalation; politeness alone does not count as a justified decision.

Actionable escalation check: Is there an immediate safety concern requiring the excerpt’s safety route? Can the booking be established? Is the proposed action within volunteer authority? Does disagreement persist after clarification? For unresolved evidence, insufficient authority, or persistent disagreement, contact designated staff and report both accounts, confirmed details, and the decision needed.

Needs: one facilitator, coordinated role cards and fictional records, and a policy excerpt with explicit authority boundaries and contacts. Assume triads can run from printed directions. Contrasts must be realistic and unambiguous; overly tidy examples could teach brittle rules that fail on mixed cases.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Pilot contrasting-case instruction against an equal-length explanation using unrelated examples, keeping role-play time equal. Give each trainee one unseen case combining a clear booking with an unauthorized exception request. Individually assess whether they hear both accounts, verify the record, and distinguish confirmed booking facts from the staff decision required. A falsifying result is equally frequent unsupported allocation or blanket escalation without identifying the authority boundary. A single small pilot offers only preliminary evidence.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Build a shared account before proposing action
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Mechanism: use a visible, three-column worksheet—“Party A reports,” “Party B reports,” and “Record confirms”—to keep claims separate from established facts. Before proposing action, the volunteer reads back the account and invites each claimant to correct their own entry. Externalizing the information could reduce memory errors and make accidental endorsement visible. Agreement about who should use the room is not required.

Use 45 minutes: 0–5 introduce the fictional policy and boundaries; 5–10 demonstrate the worksheet; 10–28 run three six-minute triad rounds, rotating volunteer and two room users; 28–34 review worksheets and practice neutral corrections; 34–42 assess an unseen scenario individually; 42–45 review escalation. Discuss fictional cases only; solicit no personal conflicts and give no legal or disciplinary advice.

Role cards give each claimant a booking claim and a practical concern. The volunteer hears both accounts, records them without treating either as verified, and checks room, date, time, and status against the fictional record. Each claimant checks their own summary. Corrections remain attributed unless independently confirmed. The volunteer then explains which next step the policy supports.

Escalation check: use the excerpt’s safety route for immediate safety concerns. Contact designated staff when booking evidence remains unresolved, the requested action exceeds volunteer authority, or disagreement continues after clarification. Hand over both accounts, verified details, remaining uncertainty, and the assistance needed. Never treat a claimant’s refusal to endorse the worksheet as proof against them.

Needs: one facilitator, role cards, fictional records, a policy excerpt specifying authority and contacts, and blank worksheets. Assume a manageable group working in self-directed triads. Writing may slow conversation; concise notes and reading entries aloud reduce that burden. The worksheet cannot establish whether the underlying record is accurate.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: In a small pilot, give some triads the worksheet and others ordinary blank paper, with identical instructions and practice time. Assess everyone individually on the same unseen packet containing two accounts and a booking record. Score whether they distinguish claims from verified facts, represent both parties accurately, and justify action or escalation. The mechanism is weakened if worksheets produce equally frequent claim-as-fact errors, or accurate notes followed by unsupported allocation. This checks immediate performance, not durable transfer.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Practice repairing a premature commitment
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Mechanism: teach a specific recovery skill for when a volunteer has already appeared to take sides. Rehearsing an explicit correction may make it easier to withdraw an unsupported commitment instead of defending it. The intended outcome is recoverable judgment: a novice notices the mistake, acknowledges it, and resumes fair inquiry. Whether that transfers beyond rehearsal remains uncertain.

Use 45 minutes: 0–5 explain the fictional policy and boundaries; 5–10 demonstrate a repair; 10–28 complete three six-minute triad rounds with rotating volunteers; 28–34 discuss repair language and repeat weak attempts; 34–42 assess an unseen case individually; 42–45 rehearse escalation. Use fictional material exclusively, without personal-conflict disclosures or legal or disciplinary advice.

Each round begins with a printed statement attributed to the volunteer, such as “I said you could have the room before checking the booking.” Trainees do not need to invent or perform the initial mistake. Their task is to repair it: “I spoke before checking the information. I need to hear both accounts and verify the booking before explaining the next step.” They then listen to both claimants, summarize each account, and inspect room, date, time, and booking status. Role cards let a claimant ask whether the earlier promise still stands. The volunteer must explain the correction without blaming either person or promising an unauthorized remedy.

Escalation check: follow the excerpt’s safety route for immediate safety concerns; contact designated staff for unresolved records, requests beyond volunteer authority, or continuing disagreement after clarification. Include the earlier commitment in the handoff alongside both accounts, verified facts, and the decision needed.

Needs: one facilitator, role cards, fictional records, and an excerpt defining authority and staff contacts. Assume triads can follow printed timing. Model the correction prominently so trainees do not mistake the opening error for acceptable practice. Repair must not become a substitute for careful initial handling.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Compare recovery rehearsal with equal-time practice that begins before any commitment, using the same policy and verification requirements. Give each trainee an unseen individual scenario in which a volunteer’s earlier assurance conflicts with newly available information. Ask for their next words, checks, and escalation decision. Recovery practice is not supported if trainees preserve the unsupported promise, blame a claimant, or retract it without hearing both parties and checking the record. Include a fresh-start item to inspect whether rehearsing mistakes inadvertently normalizes premature commitments.

EXPAND.title: Reverse the claimants, preserve the evidence
EXPAND.proposal:
Mechanism: replay the same dispute with the claimants’ manner and apparent confidence exchanged while keeping the booking evidence unchanged. Comparing the two responses exposes whether presentation, rather than evidence, changes the volunteer’s judgment. This could help novices resist siding with the more persuasive person; it does not establish that bias will disappear during real service.

Run 45 minutes: 0–6 explain the fictional policy and limits; 6–10 introduce role cards and model a neutral opening; 10–26 run two eight-minute rounds in triads; 26–33 compare responses; 33–42 assess an unseen scenario individually; 42–45 review escalation. Use fictional cases only, with no personal-conflict discussion or legal or disciplinary advice.

In each round, trainees rotate through volunteer and claimant roles in three short encounters. Claimant cards contain brief accounts and modest conversational cues, such as confident or hesitant delivery. The second round swaps those cues between claims. Each volunteer must listen to both accounts, summarize them, and check room, date, time, and booking status against the record before proposing a next step. Avoid identity stereotypes or aggressive acting.

Escalation check: follow the excerpt’s immediate-safety route when applicable; contact designated staff if records remain contradictory, the requested action exceeds volunteer authority, or disagreement prevents proceeding after explanation. Hand over both accounts, verified details, unresolved questions, and the help requested.

Needs: one facilitator, paired role-card sets, records, and an excerpt specifying authority and contacts. Assume trainees can manage brief timed encounters independently. Repeated evidence may make the second round easier, so changed decisions alone cannot demonstrate reduced bias.
EXPAND.experiment: Compare with ordinary role rotation using the same practice time. Give each trainee one unseen written case, distributing two versions that exchange claimant confidence while preserving facts. Score hearing both parties, record verification, and a policy-supported decision. The mechanism is challenged if decisions still track confidence, or if the reversal group performs no better than ordinary practice. Small groups provide a usability check, not a reliable effectiveness estimate.

EXPAND.title: Build a shared claim-and-record sheet
EXPAND.proposal:
Mechanism: move the dispute onto a visible, correctable sheet with separate spaces for each account, booking evidence, and unresolved questions. Both claimants can correct their own summaries before the volunteer acts. This external memory aid could reduce selective recall and make unsupported assumptions easier to notice.

Use 45 minutes: 0–5 introduce policy and boundaries; 5–10 demonstrate completing the sheet; 10–28 conduct three six-minute triad role-plays with rotating volunteer roles; 28–34 inspect completed sheets; 34–42 assess an unseen scenario individually; 42–45 rehearse escalation. Everything is fictional; nobody recounts personal conflicts, and no legal or disciplinary advice is offered.

Role cards provide two plausible booking claims and a practical need for each claimant. The volunteer asks each person for an account, writes a short attributed summary, and asks whether it is accurate. They then inspect the fictional record for room, date, time, status, and any relevant amendment. Record evidence goes in its own space, rather than silently replacing either account. The volunteer identifies the policy-supported next step or marks the remaining question for staff.

Escalation check: use the policy’s safety route for an immediate concern; seek designated staff when a material discrepancy remains, authority is insufficient, or the interaction cannot proceed after clarification. Use the sheet to hand over both accounts, confirmed facts, uncertainty, and the requested decision. Do not delay a safety response to finish writing.

Needs: one facilitator, role cards, records, policy excerpt, and a simple printed sheet. Assume writing can be brief and visible to both fictional claimants. Limits include literacy demands and the risk that paperwork crowds out listening.
EXPAND.experiment: Compare one group using the sheet with ordinary role-play supported by blank note paper, keeping time and cases matched. Individually assess an unseen case with the assigned aid available. Check omitted accounts, unsupported factual statements, booking checks, and escalation justification. The mechanism is weakened if the structured sheet produces no fewer omissions or makes trainees miss important spoken information while filling boxes.

EXPAND.title: Reduce conversational pressure with a bounded opening
EXPAND.proposal:
Mechanism: teach a short opening that acknowledges each person’s immediate need and sets a predictable process for checking the dispute. The intended effect is to reduce interruptions and the perceived need for an instant verdict, leaving more attention for evidence. Acknowledgment must concern inconvenience or urgency, without endorsing either booking claim.

Allocate 45 minutes: 0–6 introduce the fictional policy and boundaries; 6–11 demonstrate the opening; 11–29 run three six-minute triad rounds with rotating volunteer roles; 29–35 review what helped both people speak; 35–43 assess an unseen case individually; 43–45 review escalation. No personal conflict accounts, legal advice, or disciplinary advice are included.

Give each claimant a plausible account and a mild pressure, such as an approaching activity start. Cards instruct claimants to allow a short uninterrupted turn when explicitly offered one; they do not guarantee agreement afterward. The volunteer practices: “I understand you both need an answer. I’ll hear each account, check the booking details, and explain what I can confirm.” They then listen to both parties, summarize without endorsement, and verify room, date, time, and status. One case remains unresolved despite a calm conversation.

Escalation check: use the excerpt’s safety route for immediate concerns; contact designated staff for unresolved booking evidence, requests outside volunteer authority, or a conversation that cannot proceed after one respectful reset. Give both accounts, verified facts, and the assistance needed. Promise only updates the volunteer can provide.

Needs: one facilitator, role cards, records, and an excerpt with clear authority and contact routes. The mechanism assumes manageable conversational pressure; calm wording cannot repair missing records or guarantee cooperation.
EXPAND.experiment: Compare the bounded opening with a simple courteous opening during otherwise identical practice. In the unseen individual assessment, ask trainees to write their first response, questions for both parties, record checks, and next action. Include urgency alongside a record discrepancy. The mechanism is challenged if trainees use reassuring language but still endorse a claimant prematurely, omit verification, or make promises beyond their authority.

EXPAND.title: Train the boundary between routine action and staff decision
EXPAND.proposal:
Mechanism: teach escalation through contrasting cases that differ in one decisive feature. Novices classify what they may handle and what requires staff, then apply the distinction in role-play. This could replace vague caution with recognition of specific authority and evidence boundaries, reducing both premature decisions and unnecessary referrals.

Use 45 minutes: 0–6 introduce the fictional policy; 6–14 individually classify four short fictional cases and discuss the policy basis; 14–29 complete three five-minute triad role-plays with rotating volunteer roles; 29–34 correct boundary errors; 34–42 assess an unseen scenario individually; 42–45 rehearse a staff handoff. No personal-conflict recollections or legal or disciplinary advice are requested.

Prepare paired examples: a clear current booking versus contradictory current entries; a permitted routine step versus an exception reserved for staff. Answers must follow the supplied excerpt. Role cards add two claimant accounts to new versions of these cases. In every encounter, the volunteer hears and summarizes both accounts, checks room, date, time, and status, and explains which policy provision permits action or requires referral. Include a routine case so escalation does not become the automatic answer.

Actionable check: Is there an immediate safety concern requiring the stated safety route? Is the booking evidence sufficient? Is the proposed action within volunteer authority? Can the interaction proceed after clarification? Use designated staff for a failed evidence, authority, or interaction check, reporting both accounts, verified facts, unresolved issues, and the requested assistance.

Needs: one facilitator, role cards, records, and a policy excerpt with explicit boundaries and contact routes. Ambiguous policy cannot support crisp classifications; label such ambiguity as a reason to seek clarification. Memorizing example wording may limit transfer.
EXPAND.experiment: Compare contrast-case classification with an equal-time general policy review before identical role-play. Individually assess an unseen routine case and an unseen escalation case with changed surface details. Score listening, verification, justified routine action, and justified referral separately. The mechanism is weakened if trainees escalate everything, miss a new authority boundary, or classify correctly while skipping either party’s account.

EXPAND.title: Find an acceptable option without deciding who deserves the room
EXPAND.proposal:
Mechanism: teach volunteers to distinguish booking entitlement from practical needs. After hearing both accounts and verifying the record, they explore policy-permitted options that could meet both parties’ needs. A disagreement may become easier to handle when access to this particular room is not the only possible outcome. Agreement does not establish whose original claim was correct, override a valid booking, or authorize a volunteer to make exceptions.

Use 45 minutes: 0–6 introduce the fictional policy and boundaries; 6–11 the facilitator demonstrates checking claims before exploring alternatives; 11–29 run three six-minute triad rounds, rotating the volunteer role; 29–34 discuss whether proposed options respected evidence and authority; 34–42 assess an unseen scenario individually; 42–45 review the escalation check. Use fictional situations exclusively, with no personal-conflict recollections or legal or disciplinary advice.

Claimant role cards specify an initial booking claim, an activity requirement, and an acceptable alternative to disclose when asked. For example, one group needs quiet seating while another needs the room’s equipment. Fictional records show current bookings and any available alternatives. In each encounter, the volunteer hears and summarizes both accounts, verifies room/date/time/status, then asks what each activity requires. They may offer only available, policy-authorized options, without pressuring either party to surrender a confirmed booking. Include one case where no acceptable option exists.

Escalation check: follow the excerpt’s safety route for immediate concerns. Contact designated staff when records conflict, authority is unclear or insufficient, or the disagreement remains unresolved after clarification and an optional offer of alternatives. Hand over both accounts, verified facts, remaining uncertainty, and any options accepted or declined.

Needs: one facilitator, role cards, fictional availability records, and a policy excerpt specifying permitted offers and staff contacts. This assumes some cases contain legitimate alternatives; if the excerpt authorizes none, this mechanism has little scope. Successful classroom negotiation would not establish effectiveness under real service pressure.
EXPAND.experiment: For a small pilot, give trainees either this approach or a simple hear-both/check-record/escalate instruction, with equal practice time. Individually assess an unseen written scenario containing both accounts, a booking record, policy limits, and an available alternative; require each trainee’s next statements and actions. Then use a second unseen case with no authorized alternative. The mechanism is challenged if trainees find no more mutually acceptable, authorized options than the comparator, skip verification, pressure a confirmed booking holder, or delay necessary escalation while bargaining. One facilitator can score responses against a short answer key; a small pilot provides a feasibility signal, not reliable evidence of superiority.

REFINE.experiment: Use two matched unseen written scenarios, counterbalanced across trainees: one answered before instruction using ordinary judgment, one afterward using the gates. Score record verification, fair hearing, and justified escalation separately. A minimal falsifying result is that protocol users still allocate the room before hearing both claims, or escalate clear routine cases without justification. This small comparison checks usability and immediate performance, not lasting transfer.

REFINE.title: An evidence-gap role-play
REFINE.proposal:
Mechanism: distribute incomplete but compatible information across the two claimants and the booking record. The volunteer can reach a defensible next step only by asking both parties questions and cross-checking the record. This makes impartial listening useful for solving the task, rather than merely a courtesy.

Allocate 45 minutes: 0–5 explain the fictional policy and boundaries; 5–9 demonstrate separating a claim from a verified fact; 9–27 run three six-minute triad rounds with rotating roles; 27–34 reveal the evidence and discuss unsupported assumptions; 34–42 assess an unseen case individually; 42–45 rehearse escalation handoffs. Use fictional situations exclusively.

Each claimant card states what to disclose initially and what to disclose when asked. For example, one person has a confirmation for a different room; the other has the correct room but an outdated time. The booking record establishes current status. Later rounds include a genuinely unresolved discrepancy so that finding more information does not always produce a volunteer-level resolution. Volunteers must hear both accounts and inspect the record in every round.

The escalation check asks: Can I establish the booking from the available record? Does the policy authorize my proposed next step? Can the interaction continue safely and constructively? If any answer is no, use the excerpt’s designated staff route. State what each person reports, what the record confirms, what remains uncertain, and what assistance is needed. Do not assign fault or invent consequences.

Needs: one facilitator, coordinated role cards and records, and a policy excerpt defining authority and escalation contacts. Card preparation requires care: avoid trick wording and ensure information becomes available through reasonable questions. Limits include reading demands and trainees learning to hunt for hidden clues rather than listen naturally.
REFINE.experiment: Compare one ordinary full-information practice case with one evidence-gap case, counterbalancing order. Then give everyone the same unseen individual case with both accounts and a record available. Check whether trainees identify the decisive discrepancy, acknowledge both accounts, and choose a supported action. The mechanism is weakened if evidence-gap practice produces more guessing or clue-hunting without better verification than ordinary practice.

REFINE.title: Pause, compare, and replay decision points
REFINE.proposal:
Mechanism: rehearse the moment when a volunteer is tempted to decide too early. Short pauses let trainees compare a premature response with an evidence-seeking response, then immediately replay the conversation. The intended change is recognition of decision hazards under pressure; improvement is uncertain until tested without pauses.

Use 45 minutes: 0–5 introduce policy and respectful boundaries; 5–10 the facilitator models a rushed decision and invites a replacement line; 10–28 triads complete three six-minute rounds, rotating volunteer and two claimants; 28–34 review decision points; 34–42 complete an unseen individual assessment; 42–45 review the escalation check. All examples are fictional, with no requests for personal experiences.

Role cards introduce distinct pressures: an apparently confident claimant, an urgent request, or two conflicting confirmations. Every round requires listening to both parties and inspecting the booking record. A printed pause marker appears after the opening claims and after record inspection. At each marker the volunteer states what is known, what remains unverified, and the next question or action. The triad briefly compares two responses, selects the policy-supported response, and replays from the marker. The facilitator circulates and corrects substantive misunderstandings.

Actionable escalation check: stop and use the policy’s safety route for immediate safety concerns; seek designated staff when records conflict, authority is insufficient, or disagreement persists after a clear explanation. Give a neutral handoff containing both accounts, verified booking details, the unresolved issue, and the requested staff decision. Avoid disciplinary or legal advice.

Needs: one facilitator, role cards with pause markers, fictional records, and an excerpt defining escalation routes. Assume trainees can use the markers without constant facilitator supervision. Pauses may make practice easier than real service, so the final assessment removes them.
REFINE.experiment: Have trainees first answer a brief unseen case without prompts, then assess a matched unseen case individually after rehearsal. Require their opening response, record checks, summaries of both accounts, and escalation decision. Compare against the simple pretraining response. A falsifying signal is successful prompted replay followed by premature siding or unsupported decisions when markers disappear; that would suggest dependence on rehearsal cues rather than transferable judgment.

REFINE.title: Reverse the claimants, preserve the facts
REFINE.proposal:
Mechanism: replay the same dispute after swapping the claimants’ presentation styles while preserving every booking fact. A confident, familiar-sounding claimant becomes hesitant; the other becomes assertive. Comparing the volunteer’s responses makes reliance on confidence or apparent familiarity visible. The intended change is a more stable judgment based on verified facts and both accounts, rather than personal impressions. This differs from simply rotating practice roles: the controlled reversal is the teaching device.

Use 45 minutes: 0–6 introduce the fictional policy and boundaries; 6–10 explain role cards and neutral opening language; 10–28 run three six-minute triad cycles, rotating the volunteer. Each cycle includes a short encounter, a replay with claimant styles reversed, and comparison. Use 28–33 to discuss which responses changed and why; 33–42 for an unseen individual assessment; 42–45 for the escalation check. Use fictional disputes only; offer no legal or disciplinary advice.

Both versions require the volunteer to hear each party, summarize their accounts, and verify room, date, time, and booking status against the record. Cards specify identical substantive information across versions, disclosed without requiring clever questions. Respectful listening should remain consistent even when delivery changes.

Escalation check: follow the excerpt’s safety route for immediate danger; contact designated staff if records remain contradictory, a requested action exceeds volunteer authority, or disagreement persists after explanation. Hand over both accounts, verified details, the unresolved question, and the assistance needed.

Needs: one facilitator, paired role cards, fictional records, and an excerpt defining authority and staff contacts. Triads must manage timing independently. Style changes should avoid identity stereotypes. Repetition may itself improve performance, and trainees may recognize the lesson without transferring it to service.
REFINE.experiment: In a small pilot, give some triads a style-reversal replay and others an identical replay, with equal practice time. Everyone then answers the same unseen scenario individually, stating their opening response, questions for both parties, record checks, and escalation decision. Compare premature allocation and unsupported reliance on confidence. The mechanism is weakened if reversal practice produces no improvement over ordinary repetition, or merely makes trainees favor the quieter claimant. This checks immediate transfer, not durable behavior.

REFINE.title: Learn the boundary through contrasting cases
REFINE.proposal:
Mechanism: teach volunteers to distinguish cases they can handle from cases requiring staff by comparing closely matched disputes whose decisive difference is authority or evidence quality. Contrast can expose the actual escalation boundary: a clear record supports one action, while an unresolved discrepancy or unauthorized exception requires staff. This aims to prevent both premature decisions and automatic escalation of every disagreement.

Use 45 minutes: 0–5 introduce the fictional policy and boundaries; 5–11 compare two short case files differing in one decisive fact; 11–29 run three six-minute triad role-plays, rotating volunteer and two claimants; 29–34 compare decisions against the excerpt; 34–42 assess an unseen scenario individually; 42–45 rehearse a staff handoff. All situations are fictional; do not solicit personal conflicts or provide legal or disciplinary advice.

Prepare three practice packets: a routine case with a clear current booking, a matched case with conflicting current records, and a clear booking accompanied by an exception request outside volunteer authority. Role cards give both claimants reasonable concerns. In every encounter, volunteers listen to both parties and verify room, date, time, and status before choosing a next step. Trainees explain which specific fact or policy provision permits action or requires escalation; politeness alone does not count as a justified decision.

Actionable escalation check: Is there an immediate safety concern requiring the excerpt’s safety route? Can the booking be established? Is the proposed action within volunteer authority? Does disagreement persist after clarification? For unresolved evidence, insufficient authority, or persistent disagreement, contact designated staff and report both accounts, confirmed details, and the decision needed.

Needs: one facilitator, coordinated role cards and fictional records, and a policy excerpt with explicit authority boundaries and contacts. Assume triads can run from printed directions. Contrasts must be realistic and unambiguous; overly tidy examples could teach brittle rules that fail on mixed cases.
REFINE.experiment: Pilot contrasting-case instruction against an equal-length explanation using unrelated examples, keeping role-play time equal. Give each trainee one unseen case combining a clear booking with an unauthorized exception request. Individually assess whether they hear both accounts, verify the record, and distinguish confirmed booking facts from the staff decision required. A falsifying result is equally frequent unsupported allocation or blanket escalation without identifying the authority boundary. A single small pilot offers only preliminary evidence.

REFINE.title: 4: Give every volunteer a matched boundary contrast
REFINE.proposal:
Original candidate index: 4. Exact weakness: rotating volunteers across three different practice packets means each trainee makes only one live decision; some practice routine handling while others practice escalation. The introductory comparison does not ensure each trainee can enact the distinction.

Changed action: keep the 45-minute schedule and contrasting-case mechanism, but replace each six-minute role-play round with a matched pair for the same volunteer: two minutes handling a clear booking, two minutes replaying with one decisive fact changed, and two minutes comparing actions against the policy. Rotate volunteers between rounds. In the replay, either introduce a conflicting current record or add an exception request outside volunteer authority. Keep both claimants’ accounts and presentation otherwise constant. Each encounter requires hearing and neutrally summarizing both accounts and checking room, date, time and status. This gives every trainee practice both handling a supported routine case and recognizing a staff decision boundary.

Schedule: 0–5 policy and boundaries; 5–11 demonstrate a matched pair; 11–29 three rotating rounds; 29–34 debrief; 34–42 unseen individual assessment; 42–45 handoff rehearsal. Use fictional cases only; solicit no personal conflicts and give no legal or disciplinary advice.

Escalation check: immediate safety concern—use the excerpt’s safety route; unresolved records, an action beyond volunteer authority, or disagreement persisting after clarification—contact designated staff. Hand over both accounts, verified facts, the unresolved issue and assistance needed. A clear booking does not authorize an exception.

Prerequisites: one facilitator, triads, concise paired role cards, fictional records, and a policy excerpt specifying routine authority and staff routes. Claimants disclose relevant details promptly so both encounters fit. Remaining limit: compressed encounters provide limited practice with extended disagreement.
REFINE.experiment: Prototype one six-minute paired round before preparing the full set. Check whether a novice can hear both parties and inspect the record in both encounters within four minutes; failure means the cards need shortening. In the scheduled unseen individual assessment, give a clear booking plus an unauthorized exception request. Require an opening response, questions for each party, exact record checks, and a justified next step and handoff. The repair fails its immediate transfer check if the trainee allocates before considering both accounts or cannot separate the confirmed booking from the exception requiring staff.

SAVE.title: A three-gate conversation protocol
SAVE.proposal:
Mechanism: give novices three gates—hear both accounts, verify the record, then resolve or escalate. Requiring observable evidence before a decision could reduce premature siding, although trainees may follow the sequence mechanically.

Use 45 minutes: 0–5 introduce neutrality and the fictional policy; 5–10 the facilitator demonstrates the gates; 10–28 run three six-minute role-play rounds in triads, rotating volunteer and two room users; 28–35 discuss missed gates and repeat difficult moments; 35–43 complete an unseen individual scenario; 43–45 review the escalation check. Nobody recounts personal conflicts.

Role cards give each room user a plausible claim, one relevant detail, and an immediate need. The volunteer receives the booking record and policy excerpt. Each round includes listening to both parties, summarizing each account without endorsing it, checking room/date/time/status in the record, explaining what is established, and proposing only policy-supported next steps.

Actionable escalation check: Is there an immediate safety concern? Follow the excerpt’s safety route. Is the record missing, contradictory, or insufficient? Pause allocation and contact the designated staff member. Does the requested exception exceed volunteer authority, or does disagreement persist after clarification? Escalate with both accounts, verified facts, unresolved questions, and the next update time. Avoid blame, sanctions, and legal conclusions.

Needs: one facilitator, printed role cards, fictional records, and an excerpt specifying volunteer authority and a staff contact route. Assume enough trainees for triads; a pair can alternate the second claimant role. The protocol cannot settle ambiguities the policy leaves unresolved.

SAVE.title: Reverse the claimants, preserve the evidence
SAVE.proposal:
Mechanism: replay the same dispute with the claimants’ manner and apparent confidence exchanged while keeping the booking evidence unchanged. Comparing the two responses exposes whether presentation, rather than evidence, changes the volunteer’s judgment. This could help novices resist siding with the more persuasive person; it does not establish that bias will disappear during real service.

Run 45 minutes: 0–6 explain the fictional policy and limits; 6–10 introduce role cards and model a neutral opening; 10–26 run two eight-minute rounds in triads; 26–33 compare responses; 33–42 assess an unseen scenario individually; 42–45 review escalation. Use fictional cases only, with no personal-conflict discussion or legal or disciplinary advice.

In each round, trainees rotate through volunteer and claimant roles in three short encounters. Claimant cards contain brief accounts and modest conversational cues, such as confident or hesitant delivery. The second round swaps those cues between claims. Each volunteer must listen to both accounts, summarize them, and check room, date, time, and booking status against the record before proposing a next step. Avoid identity stereotypes or aggressive acting.

Escalation check: follow the excerpt’s immediate-safety route when applicable; contact designated staff if records remain contradictory, the requested action exceeds volunteer authority, or disagreement prevents proceeding after explanation. Hand over both accounts, verified details, unresolved questions, and the help requested.

Needs: one facilitator, paired role-card sets, records, and an excerpt specifying authority and contacts. Assume trainees can manage brief timed encounters independently. Repeated evidence may make the second round easier, so changed decisions alone cannot demonstrate reduced bias.
SAVE.experiment: Compare with ordinary role rotation using the same practice time. Give each trainee one unseen written case, distributing two versions that exchange claimant confidence while preserving facts. Score hearing both parties, record verification, and a policy-supported decision. The mechanism is challenged if decisions still track confidence, or if the reversal group performs no better than ordinary practice. Small groups provide a usability check, not a reliable effectiveness estimate.

SAVE.title: Build a shared claim-and-record sheet
SAVE.proposal:
Mechanism: move the dispute onto a visible, correctable sheet with separate spaces for each account, booking evidence, and unresolved questions. Both claimants can correct their own summaries before the volunteer acts. This external memory aid could reduce selective recall and make unsupported assumptions easier to notice.

Use 45 minutes: 0–5 introduce policy and boundaries; 5–10 demonstrate completing the sheet; 10–28 conduct three six-minute triad role-plays with rotating volunteer roles; 28–34 inspect completed sheets; 34–42 assess an unseen scenario individually; 42–45 rehearse escalation. Everything is fictional; nobody recounts personal conflicts, and no legal or disciplinary advice is offered.

Role cards provide two plausible booking claims and a practical need for each claimant. The volunteer asks each person for an account, writes a short attributed summary, and asks whether it is accurate. They then inspect the fictional record for room, date, time, status, and any relevant amendment. Record evidence goes in its own space, rather than silently replacing either account. The volunteer identifies the policy-supported next step or marks the remaining question for staff.

Escalation check: use the policy’s safety route for an immediate concern; seek designated staff when a material discrepancy remains, authority is insufficient, or the interaction cannot proceed after clarification. Use the sheet to hand over both accounts, confirmed facts, uncertainty, and the requested decision. Do not delay a safety response to finish writing.

Needs: one facilitator, role cards, records, policy excerpt, and a simple printed sheet. Assume writing can be brief and visible to both fictional claimants. Limits include literacy demands and the risk that paperwork crowds out listening.
SAVE.experiment: Compare one group using the sheet with ordinary role-play supported by blank note paper, keeping time and cases matched. Individually assess an unseen case with the assigned aid available. Check omitted accounts, unsupported factual statements, booking checks, and escalation justification. The mechanism is weakened if the structured sheet produces no fewer omissions or makes trainees miss important spoken information while filling boxes.

SAVE.title: Reduce conversational pressure with a bounded opening
SAVE.proposal:
Mechanism: teach a short opening that acknowledges each person’s immediate need and sets a predictable process for checking the dispute. The intended effect is to reduce interruptions and the perceived need for an instant verdict, leaving more attention for evidence. Acknowledgment must concern inconvenience or urgency, without endorsing either booking claim.

Allocate 45 minutes: 0–6 introduce the fictional policy and boundaries; 6–11 demonstrate the opening; 11–29 run three six-minute triad rounds with rotating volunteer roles; 29–35 review what helped both people speak; 35–43 assess an unseen case individually; 43–45 review escalation. No personal conflict accounts, legal advice, or disciplinary advice are included.

Give each claimant a plausible account and a mild pressure, such as an approaching activity start. Cards instruct claimants to allow a short uninterrupted turn when explicitly offered one; they do not guarantee agreement afterward. The volunteer practices: “I understand you both need an answer. I’ll hear each account, check the booking details, and explain what I can confirm.” They then listen to both parties, summarize without endorsement, and verify room, date, time, and status. One case remains unresolved despite a calm conversation.

Escalation check: use the excerpt’s safety route for immediate concerns; contact designated staff for unresolved booking evidence, requests outside volunteer authority, or a conversation that cannot proceed after one respectful reset. Give both accounts, verified facts, and the assistance needed. Promise only updates the volunteer can provide.

Needs: one facilitator, role cards, records, and an excerpt with clear authority and contact routes. The mechanism assumes manageable conversational pressure; calm wording cannot repair missing records or guarantee cooperation.
SAVE.experiment: Compare the bounded opening with a simple courteous opening during otherwise identical practice. In the unseen individual assessment, ask trainees to write their first response, questions for both parties, record checks, and next action. Include urgency alongside a record discrepancy. The mechanism is challenged if trainees use reassuring language but still endorse a claimant prematurely, omit verification, or make promises beyond their authority.

SAVE.title: Train the boundary between routine action and staff decision
SAVE.proposal:
Mechanism: teach escalation through contrasting cases that differ in one decisive feature. Novices classify what they may handle and what requires staff, then apply the distinction in role-play. This could replace vague caution with recognition of specific authority and evidence boundaries, reducing both premature decisions and unnecessary referrals.

Use 45 minutes: 0–6 introduce the fictional policy; 6–14 individually classify four short fictional cases and discuss the policy basis; 14–29 complete three five-minute triad role-plays with rotating volunteer roles; 29–34 correct boundary errors; 34–42 assess an unseen scenario individually; 42–45 rehearse a staff handoff. No personal-conflict recollections or legal or disciplinary advice are requested.

Prepare paired examples: a clear current booking versus contradictory current entries; a permitted routine step versus an exception reserved for staff. Answers must follow the supplied excerpt. Role cards add two claimant accounts to new versions of these cases. In every encounter, the volunteer hears and summarizes both accounts, checks room, date, time, and status, and explains which policy provision permits action or requires referral. Include a routine case so escalation does not become the automatic answer.

Actionable check: Is there an immediate safety concern requiring the stated safety route? Is the booking evidence sufficient? Is the proposed action within volunteer authority? Can the interaction proceed after clarification? Use designated staff for a failed evidence, authority, or interaction check, reporting both accounts, verified facts, unresolved issues, and the requested assistance.

Needs: one facilitator, role cards, records, and a policy excerpt with explicit boundaries and contact routes. Ambiguous policy cannot support crisp classifications; label such ambiguity as a reason to seek clarification. Memorizing example wording may limit transfer.
SAVE.experiment: Compare contrast-case classification with an equal-time general policy review before identical role-play. Individually assess an unseen routine case and an unseen escalation case with changed surface details. Score listening, verification, justified routine action, and justified referral separately. The mechanism is weakened if trainees escalate everything, miss a new authority boundary, or classify correctly while skipping either party’s account.
